Severe Flooding Halts Operations Across Italian Metals & Mining Sites

Widespread flooding in northern Italy has brought significant disruption to the country’s Metals & Mining industry, with multiple sites reporting suspended operations and substantial damage as heavy rains continue for a fifth consecutive day. The unprecedented rainfall has caused rivers to overflow in the Lombardy and Veneto regions, submerging open-pit mines, processing plants, and storage facilities.

According to the Italian Association of Metals & Mining Producers (IAMMP), at least seven major mining and smelting operations have halted production since Monday. "The flooding has rendered access roads within our sites impassable, and several of our extraction pits are now submerged," said Massimo Ferrara, chief operating officer of Valtaro Minerals, one of the region’s largest operators. "Our priority is the safety of our workforce and the protection of our assets, but the situation remains extremely challenging."

IAMMP estimates that over 1,200 employees across member companies have been evacuated from operational areas due to rising water and the risk of landslides. Union representatives report that around 250 contract workers have been temporarily placed on paid leave. "We are in close contact with management to ensure the safety of all workers and to secure jobs during this emergency," said Francesca Romano, spokesperson for the National Union of Miners and Metallurgists.

Industry analysts warn that prolonged flooding could delay planned shipments of copper, zinc, and rare earth elements. "Storage yards containing processed metals are under water, and there is significant concern about contamination and material loss," said Filippo Tosetti, senior analyst at ItalRes Consulting. "If water levels do not recede soon, companies may face weeks of cleanup before resuming normal operations."

Company officials from AlpiMet, a major refiner in the region, report that smelting furnaces have been shut down as a precaution. "Our technical teams are monitoring the facility around the clock for structural damage and to prevent electrical hazards," said chief engineer Lucia Pagani.

With meteorologists forecasting continued rainfall over the next 48 hours, Metals & Mining companies have begun deploying emergency pumps and protective barriers at vulnerable sites. However, IAMMP cautions that persistent precipitation could exacerbate soil instability, heightening the risk of further landslides near hillside mines.

"We are dealing with a highly dynamic emergency," said IAMMP president Paolo Riva. "Our industry is coordinating closely to share resources and technical expertise as we respond to this crisis."
